paper_a.title: Simultaneous Analysis of Lasso and Dantzig Selector

paper_b.title: On asymptotically optimal confidence regions and tests for high-dimensional models

metadata.description: Both papers address high-dimensional linear regression with the lasso, but pursue substantially different goals: paper A (Bickel-Ritov-Tsybakov 2009) builds the estimation-error machinery — RE conditions, oracle inequalities, $\ell_p$ coefficient bounds — for the Lasso and the Dantzig selector and proves the two are nearly equivalent. Paper B (van de Geer-Buhlmann-Ritov-Dezeure 2014) targets statistical inference: it constructs the desparsified-lasso pivot via nodewise regression to obtain asymptotically Gaussian, semiparametrically efficient confidence intervals for individual coefficients in linear and GLM settings. Paper B uses BRT-style $\ell_1$-bounds (cited to Buhlmann-vdG 2011) and a compatibility condition (a relative of BRT's RE) as inputs but introduces an entirely new debiasing/inference framework with no counterpart in BRT. The relationship is therefore competing/complementary frameworks (CF) — same core estimator, fundamentally different theoretical machinery, with paper A's results appearing as cited prior work inside paper B.

matches.explanation: Both papers set up the regression model. Paper A starts in nonparametric Gaussian regression with a finite dictionary $\mathcal F_M=\{f_1,\dots,f_M\}$ (DP4.1) and the induced design matrix (DP4.2). Paper B starts directly in the high-dimensional linear model $Y=\bx\beta^0+\varepsilon$ with $p>n$ and sparse active set $S_0$ (DP20.1). Paper A reduces to the linear model in Section 6 (used by TP4.4-TP4.6), at which point the two setups coincide up to notation ($M\leftrightarrow p$, $f_j\leftrightarrow X_{\cdot j}$). Analogous because A is more general (nonparametric framing) but specializes to B's setting.

Paper A's sparsity index $\mathcal M(\beta)=\#\{j:\beta_j\ne 0\}$ with $J(\beta)$ (DP4.4) is the same notion as paper B's active set $S_0=\{j:\beta_j^0\ne 0\}$ with $s_0=|S_0|$ (embedded inside DP20.1). Identical mathematical object up to letter choice.

Paper A defines the empirical norm $\|g\|_n$ (DP4.3) and the Gram matrix $\Psi_n=X^TX/n$ with extremal eigenvalues (DP4.5). Paper B uses $\hat\Sigma=\bx^T\bx/n$ and the empirical $\ell_2$ norm throughout but does not extract them as standalone definition nodes; the closest paper-origin definition referencing $\hat\Sigma$ is DP20.5 (desparsified lasso, which is built from $\hat\Sigma$ and its approximate inverse). Listed as low-confidence analogous because paper B simply imports the empirical Gram via DP20.5 rather than treating it as a contribution.

Paper A's restricted eigenvalues $\phi_{\min}(u),\phi_{\max}(u)$ over submatrices of size $\le u$ (DP4.6) and restricted correlations $\theta_{m_1,m_2}$ between disjoint index subsets (DP4.7) are BRT-specific design quantities used to derive sufficient conditions for the RE assumption. Paper B uses the compatibility constant $\phi_0$ and the population min-eigenvalue $\Lambda_{\min}$ but never restricted-correlations or BRT-style submatrix eigenvalues.

Paper A's weak sparsity property (DP4.8) is a nonparametric-regression notion: it requires a sparse $\beta$ whose bias term is dominated by a multiple of the variance term. Paper B works in a fully linear/GLM model with a true sparse $\beta^0$ and no analogous bias-controlling definition.

Paper A's restricted-eigenvalue assumptions RE$(s,c_0)$ (AssumP4.1) and RE$(s,m,c_0)$ (AssumP4.2) and paper B's compatibility condition (DP20.4, used inside AssumP20.1) are the same family of identifiability conditions on the empirical Gram matrix: positive lower bound on $\beta^T\hat\Sigma\beta/\|\beta_{S_0}\|^2$ over the cone $\|\beta_{S_0^c}\|_1\le c_0\|\beta_{S_0}\|_1$. They differ in normalisation (compatibility uses $\|\beta_{S_0}\|_1$, RE uses $|\beta_{J_0}|_2$) and compatibility is a strictly weaker condition implied by RE. DP20.4 is paper B's external-origin definition (van de Geer 2007). Analogous (not exact) because of the $\ell_1/\ell_2$ normalisation difference; paper A's contribution is the prior-work form referenced by paper B.

Paper A's Assumptions 1-5 give sufficient conditions for the RE assumption in terms of restricted eigenvalues and mutual coherence. Paper B never invokes any of these BRT-specific sufficient conditions — it simply assumes compatibility (or population min-eigenvalue) directly.

Paper A's Lasso optimization (ProbP4.1) and Lasso estimator algorithm (AP4.1) and paper B's Lasso definition (DP20.2) are the same $\ell_1$-penalized least-squares estimator. Paper A uses weighted penalty $2r\sum_j \|f_j\|_n |\beta_j|$ while paper B uses $2\lambda\|\beta\|_1$; with normalized columns $\|f_j\|_n=1$ they coincide. DP20.2 is paper B's external-origin definition (Tibshirani 1996); paper A's restatement is the same canonical estimator.
The Dantzig selector (ProbP4.2, AP4.2) is one of the two estimators paper A simultaneously analyses but plays no role in paper B's framework, which is built around the lasso and its desparsification.

Both encode the lasso's first-order optimality. Paper A's EP4.1 states the consequence $|D^{-1/2}X^T(y-X\hat\beta_L)/n|_\infty\le r$ (the KKT residual sup-bound, also showing the Lasso solution satisfies the Dantzig constraint). Paper B's DP20.3 states the full subgradient form $-\bx^T(Y-\bx\hat\beta)/n+\lambda\hat\kappa=0$ with $\|\hat\kappa\|_\infty\le 1$. Different formulations of the same KKT system. Paper B's DP20.3 retains the subgradient $\hat\kappa$ explicitly because it is the carrier of the bias-correction term in the desparsified estimator.

Paper A's cone condition $|\bD_{J_0^c}|_1\le c_0|\bD_{J_0}|_1$ (EP4.2) and Lasso cone Corollary B.1 ($c_0=3$, CP4.2) are the same cone restriction that appears inside paper B's compatibility-condition definition (DP20.4 uses exactly $\|\beta_{S_0^c}\|_1\le 3\|\beta_{S_0}\|_1$). The cone shape is identical; in paper A it is a derived property of $\hat\beta_L-\beta$ and $\hat\beta_D-\beta$, while in paper B it is the universal-quantifier set built into the compatibility definition.

Paper A's Lemma 4.1 (restricted positive definiteness, LP4.1) shows that Assumptions 1 and 2 imply RE$(s,c_0)$ and RE$(s,m,c_0)$ with explicit constants $\kappa_1,\kappa_2$. Paper B has no analogue of these inter-assumption implications; it treats compatibility as a primitive.

Paper A's Lemma B.1 is the basic Lasso oracle inequality (prediction-loss + $\ell_1$-error bound + sup-bound on residual + sparsity bound), all on the high-probability event $\A$. Paper B does not state an oracle inequality of this form as a paper-origin contribution; the closest object is the cited external $\ell_1$-bound LP20.3, which is much weaker than the full LP4.2.
Paper A's Lemma B.2 controls the Dantzig cone and residual sup-bound. Since paper B does not consider the Dantzig selector, there is no counterpart.
BRT's Theorems 1-2 establish near-equivalence of Lasso and Dantzig prediction loss. Paper B never compares estimators in this sense (it has no Dantzig analysis).

BRT's Theorem 3 is the sparsity oracle inequality for Lasso prediction in nonparametric regression. Paper B works in an exact linear/GLM model and does not produce an oracle inequality; the lasso $\ell_1$-rate is imported only as a tool (LP20.3).
BRT's Proposition 1 is the Dantzig sparsity oracle inequality in the nonparametric regression setting. No analogue in paper B.
BRT's Theorems 4 and 6 give Dantzig coefficient $\ell_p$ bounds (and a sup-form). Paper B has no Dantzig results.

Paper A's Theorem 5 (Lasso coefficient bounds in the linear model with unit Gram diagonal: $\ell_1$ bound $|\hat\beta-\beta^*|_1\le \frac{16A}{\kappa^2}\sigma s\sqrt{\log M/n}$, prediction $\ell_2$ bound $|X(\hat\beta-\beta^*)|_2^2\le \frac{16A^2}{\kappa^2}\sigma^2 s\log M$) and paper B's Lemma 5.1 ($\|\hat\beta-\beta^0\|_1\le 8\lambda s_0/\phi_0^2$, $\|\bx(\hat\beta-\beta^0)\|_2^2/n\le 8\lambda^2 s_0/\phi_0^2$) are the same canonical $\ell_1$/prediction bounds for the lasso. LP20.3 is paper B's external citation (Buhlmann-vdG 2011 Theorem 6.1), which is itself a packaging of BRT's Theorem 5 / Theorem 7.2 — direct prior-work alignment. Constants and exact RE/compatibility constant differ (RE $\kappa^2$ vs compatibility $\phi_0^2$, factor 16 vs 8) but the rates and shape are identical.
Corollary 1 (soft Lasso oracle inequality with replaced RE constant $\gamma$) is a refinement of TP4.3 specific to BRT. No analogue in paper B.

All ten proofs in paper A (PP4.1-PP4.10) prove BRT-specific results: Lemma 4.1 restricted positive definiteness, Lemma B.1 Lasso oracle inequality, Lemma B.2 Dantzig cone control, Corollary B.1, Theorems 1-5 and Proposition 1. Since the parent theorems have no paper-B counterparts, the proofs do not align. Paper B's proofs (PP20.1-PP20.7) target inference-side results (TP20.1, TP20.2, TP20.4, TP20.5, TP20.7, LP20.5, LP20.6) that have no paper-A counterparts in the opposite direction.

The desparsified-lasso estimator (linear DP20.5 and GLM DP20.10) is paper B's central new construction: $\hat b=\hat\beta+\hat\Theta\bx^T(Y-\bx\hat\beta)/n$. Paper A (2009) predates this construction and has no analogous bias-correction object.

Nodewise lasso (DP20.6 with $X^TX/n$ input, DP20.11 with arbitrary symmetric matrix input), the extended KKT conditions (DP20.7), and the nodewise-lasso algorithm (AP20.1) are tools paper B uses to construct an approximate inverse $\hat\Theta$ of $\hat\Sigma$. Paper A never inverts $\hat\Sigma$ in any approximate sense and has no analogue. (DP20.6 is also external-origin per Meinshausen-Buhlmann 2006.)
Honest-CI definition (DP20.8, external-origin Li 1989) — paper A does not consider confidence intervals at all.
$\ell_1$-penalized GLM (DP20.9). Paper A is restricted to Gaussian-noise least-squares regression and does not treat GLMs.

Random-design and GLM-regularity assumption families: (A2) Gaussian random design, (B1)-(B4) sub-Gaussian/bounded random design with row-sparsity rates, (C1)-(C8) GLM regularity, (D1)-(D5) nodewise-regression-for-random-matrices regularity. All are inference-side conditions tied to the desparsification machinery; paper A only assumes fixed design with the RE condition.

The pivot identity $\hat\beta-\beta^0+\hat\Theta\lambda\hat\kappa=\hat\Theta\bx^T\varepsilon/n-\Delta/\sqrt n$ (EP20.1) and the asymptotic-pivot statement $\sqrt n(\hat b-\beta^0)=W+o_\PP(1)$ with $W|\bx\sim\mathcal N$ (EP20.2) are the algebraic core of paper B's debiasing approach. Paper A produces no such pivot.

The Lasso-Pro (AP20.2) and Lasso-ProG (AP20.3) procedures are paper B's two executable inference algorithms: lasso fit + nodewise lasso + bias correction + Wald-type CIs. Paper A has no inference algorithm.

Paper B's main pivot-decomposition theorems for the desparsified lasso under fixed design (TP20.1), Gaussian random design (TP20.2), uniform-over-sparse-class honest convergence (CP20.1), and sub-Gaussian/bounded design (TP20.4). All are inference results with no paper-A analogue.

Theorem 2.3 (semiparametric efficiency: the desparsified lasso reaches the information bound and is regular) and Lemma 2.1 (a concrete partially-linear example satisfying the asymptotic-representation condition). These are entirely paper B contributions on the inference/efficiency side.

GLM-side asymptotic-normality results: Theorem 3.1 (CLT for desparsified GLM estimator), Theorem 3.2 (nodewise-regression rates for GLM-style random matrices), Corollary 3.1 (negligibility of nodewise errors), Lemma 3.1 (asymptotic-variance lemma), Theorem 3.3 (asymptotic normality under bounded GLM design). Paper A does not treat GLMs or asymptotic distribution theory.

Paper B's auxiliary lemmas LP20.5 ($\max_j 1/\hat\tau_j^2=\mathcal O_\PP(1)$) and LP20.6 ($\|\hat\Omega-\Theta\|_\infty=o_\PP(1)$) handle the random-design behaviour of the nodewise-residual variances and the asymptotic-variance estimate. Both are inference-pipeline lemmas with no paper-A counterpart.

All seven paper-B proofs (Theorem 2.1, 2.2, 2.4, 3.1, 3.3, Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.4) target the inference-side theorems listed above; none align with any paper-A proof since the parent results have no paper-A counterpart.
